We launched Patchwork CI with a promise to keep it free for open source, and plenty of people asked how we would make money that way. Today we run on 1,200 repositories, and about 900 of them are open source.

The number that surprised me most: across all those repos, 1 in 7 CI failures turned out to be a flaky test. That's a lot of developer hours wasted on red builds that weren't real failures.

Open source gave us more than users. It gave us data, feedback, and a community. Our most-requested feature, GitLab support, came straight from OSS maintainers, and we shipped it on November 12.

Losing our first big customer changed how Ledgerline builds. 5 months in, they walked away. It stung. A lot.

The reason: they had heavily customized their NetSuite instance, and we only supported standard fields. We weren't meeting them where they were.

So we did what we could: we listened, we learned, and we built. We spent 6 weeks adding support for custom fields. That changed how we think about our customers.

Today we serve 38 customers, and 11 of them rely on custom fields. The customer we lost told us what to build, and listening to that kind of hard feedback is what built the product we have now.

We built an app for Rotaship and nobody used it. It was sleek, modern, and we assumed restaurant staff would like it. In the first month, only 12% of staff opened it. That's when it hit us: we weren't solving the real problem. We were adding another one. Restaurant teams don't want another app. They live on WhatsApp. So in 2025 we moved everything into WhatsApp. Now 140 outlets use it, and the median reply time to shift messages is under 20 minutes. Build where your users already are. Don't make them come to you. Sometimes the best product decision is letting go of the thing you love.

#ProductManagement #Indonesia #StartupLessons #UserExperience

1,000 families now pay €4.99 a month for Pebble Pantry.

14 months ago it was just an idea I scribbled down during maternity leave, when I was sleep-deprived and staring at an empty fridge at 7pm. Today, those families use the service to make dinner time a little easier.

We didn't get here through ad campaigns or growth hacks. Most of our families found us through school WhatsApp groups, where parents recommended us to other parents. That growth came from trust, and every mum and dad who shared us in a group chat built this with us.

When we started Fernway Studio, we charged by the hour. Every agency does.

Then 4 of our first 6 projects blew past budget. Clients were frustrated. So were we. Trust was eroding.

In 2024 we switched to a fixed price: KES 450,000 per Shopify store. Now clients know exactly what they're paying, we work smarter instead of longer, and the relationship runs on trust, not timesheets.

Since then: 31 stores launched. Only 2 went over our 6-week timeline.

Founders, how do you price your services? Tell me in the comments.

I spent 11 years as a vet in a clinic, then left. I loved the work, but one thing wore me down: pets arriving so anxious we had to sedate them just to examine them. There had to be another way.

So in 2023 I started Doorstep Vet. We come to your home, where your pet feels safest, and do the exam there.

Today our team of 4 vets runs about 30 home visits a week around Melbourne. The pets stay calm. The owners relax. And I can do better medicine because of it.

Quietroom is hiring its first Account Executive. Maybe it's you.

Here's the context: we've sold 210 booths so far, every single one through founder-led sales. That got us this far. Now we need someone to take it further.

Who we want: a driven salesperson who likes a fast-moving startup, builds real relationships, and works well with a team.

What you get: £55,000 base plus commission. London-based, 3 days a week in our office. And a real say in the future of workplace focus.

If that sounds like your kind of job, we want to hear from you.

Apply via the link in the comments.

In September we raised Tabwise's price 50%, from $8 to $12 per user per month. Scariest call we've ever made.

Why raise it at all? Support costs per customer had doubled since launch. We could cut quality or charge more. We charged more.

Existing customers kept their $8 price for 12 months. We weren't going to punish the people who got us here.

Then we waited. Two months later: 2 churned customers. Out of 140.

That's the whole story. People pay for outcomes, not software. Price like you believe that.

Your turn, founders. When did you last raise your prices?

Our first production run at Shelfwise didn't go as planned. 400 labels shipped with a faulty battery contact.

As a young hardware startup, we could have cut corners. Instead, we recalled and replaced all 400 labels at our own cost, which set us back about $7,000. It was painful, but it protected the trust our customers put in us.

We also introduced a 100% contact test at the factory. Since then, we've had zero contact failures across 6,000 labels.

To other hardware founders: own your mistakes, fix them fast, and build systems so they don't happen again.

#Hardware #Startups #Manufacturing #Leadership #Integrity

$50K MRR. Bootstrapped. 18 months.

When I started Crateful, people told me I needed VC funding. That I'd never compete without a big team. That bootstrapping was too slow.

Eighteen months later: $50,000 in monthly recurring revenue, zero outside funding, a team of 3.

One channel did most of the work. The Shopify App Store brings in about 60% of our signups. We put the product where our customers were already looking, and that mattered more than anything else we tried.

If you're bootstrapping through the late nights, here's what worked for us: we chased profitability and sustainability instead of hype and vanity metrics. What helped you grow without funding?

A spindle failure shut down our line for 3 days.

Years ago I was a maintenance engineer at an auto-parts plant in Pune. A spindle failed, and the whole production line sat dead for 3 days. The vibration readings had flagged it 2 weeks earlier. Nobody was watching them.

That failure is why I started Ferrous in 2022. We monitor machines so you catch the failure before it stops your line.

Today our sensors sit on 410 machines across 17 plants. Every alert is a breakdown you don't have. Every plant brings Indian manufacturing a step closer to that.

Data only helps if someone is listening.

#Manufacturing #Industry40 #PredictiveMaintenance #MakeInIndia #StartupStory

We run Linguo Labs in three ways. First, we have a written-first culture: most work is written and reviewed asynchronously, so everyone can do deep, focused work on their own schedule. Second, we have No-Meeting Wednesdays, one full day every week for focus and recharging. Third, we meet in person twice a year in Tallinn to connect and celebrate.

We've never felt more connected as a team. What's your best tip for building a remote culture?

Why we dropped the 25% recruiting fee.

For years, Northbound Talent charged what every firm charges: 25% of first-year salary.

It never sat right with me. Our average fee ran about $41,000 per hire. If you're running an early-stage startup, that's a serious chunk of runway. And the incentives were backwards. The higher the salary, the bigger our fee. That's not partnership.

So in January we switched to a flat $18,000 per hire. No percentages.

The result: 26 senior Rust engineers placed this year, and our client relationships are stronger than ever.

The recruiting industry needs to change. You deserve better.

Would you work with a flat-fee recruiter? Tell me below.

#Recruiting #Startups #RustLang #Hiring #FutureOfWork
